newsitem.title: USA: Court ruling could save Columbus mlns - city auditor.
newsitem.headline: Court ruling could save Columbus mlns - city auditor.

text.p: Columbus, Ohio, city Auditor Hugh Dorrian said Wednesday the city will save millions if a U.S. Court of Appeals ruling on the tax status of a planned city bond issue stands.

The Court of Appeals in Washington, D.C., ruled Tuesday that the Internal Revenue Service and a U.S. Tax Court judge had erred in finding a planned Columbus bond issue ineligible for tax exempt status.
Columbus had sought to issue the debt in late 1993 to satisfy an obligation to Ohio for its creation of a state police and firefighters pension plan 30 years ago.
When Ohio took over the pension planning for municipalities in 1967, the state calculated each city's obligation to the program and found Columbus liable for $42.7 million.
The Columbus obligation had been set on a payment schedule through mid-2035, but a change in Ohio state law in 1993 permitted municipalities to pay it sooner and at a discount.

Columbus and state officials negotiated a 35 percent discount, making the city's obligation $27 million. Columbus then sought to issue the tax-exempt general obligation bonds, but held off when the Internal Revenue Service questioned the tax-exempt status the day before it was scheduled to go to market.
An IRS private letter denied tax-exempt status in 1994 and Columbus filed a lawsuit in the U.S. Tax Court challenging the decision. The Tax Court also ruled for the IRS.
The three-judge panel vacated the earlier ruling and remanded the case back to the Tax Court for further consideration.
IRS Spokesman Steve Pyrek said Wednesday that officials were still reviewing the decision and had not yet decided whether they would ask the Court of Appeals for a rehearing.
The city would have saved $13 million immediately and about $40 million in nominal dollars, Dorrian said.
Columbus privately placed $27 million of bond anticipation notes to pay off the liability and have refunded them yearly while awaiting a favorable decision.
"Obviously we have to let some time pass and find out what the decision of the lower court is and enter into some longer term financing of the note," Dorrian said.
Five or six other Ohio cities, including Cleveland, hope to issue tax-exempt bonds to take advantage of the program as well, Dorrian noted.

"It's what we thought should have been the result when we first approached this transaction so many years ago," said Daniel Rohr, managing director of public finance for Banc One Capital Corp in Columbus.
"It's always been puzzling to all of us who have been close to it how the treasury, the IRS and the Tax Court could conclude what they concluded."
Banc One, the Ohio Municipal League and the state police and fire pension fund developed the legislation permitting cities to payoff their obligation to the state.

Banc One has not had discussions with Columbus since the 1993 issue stalled, Rohr said. It has had discussions with many communities that have issued taxable obligations like Columbus as well as others that have expressed interest in the tax-exempt plan, he said.

"We have always felt that this is a current refunding, done at an arm's length distance, and certainly there is no prohibition from two parties coming to an agreement on a price to repay debt and that's what happened," Rohr said.
